opus-5.5.text:
I think harnesses are genuinely useful, and I don't want to dismiss them. But they're compensating for something, and you should ask what that is.

When you bolt external memory onto a model, a scratchpad, a vector store, a file of notes it writes to itself, you're asking the model to decide in the moment what will matter later. That's the hard part. Humans are surprisingly good at it, partly because our memory isn't a separate system we query. It's tangled up with how we perceive and reason. When I worked on protein structure, the most important things I learned weren't facts I could have written on an index card. They were intuitions about which signals to trust and which results smelled wrong. You can't easily serialize that into a text file and retrieve it with a similarity search.

So the first limitation is that the harness only preserves what the model knew to write down, and the model often doesn't know what it doesn't know. The second is brittleness. A lot of these scaffolds are hand-engineered around one model's failure modes. You build retry loops, verification steps, a planner that breaks tasks into chunks, and it works, but it's tuned to a particular set of weaknesses. When the underlying model changes, half of that machinery becomes unnecessary or actively gets in the way. There's a version of the bitter lesson here: clever structure around a learning system tends to lose to a better learning system.

The third, and probably the deepest, is that none of this changes the model. If an agent works on a problem for a week and its weights are the same at the end, then in an important sense it hasn't learned anything. It's accumulated context. That's different from getting better at the thing. A good scientist after a year on a hard problem isn't someone with a bigger notebook. They have a different mind.

So I'd say harnesses are a reasonable engineering bridge, and we'll get a lot of value out of them in the near term. But if the goal is agents that can sustain long, open-ended work like research, I suspect we'll eventually need some form of continual learning, where experience shapes the model rather than just its context. How to do that safely and stably is an open question. I just don't think you can scaffold your way all the way there.

r001.rationale: The response says harnesses accumulate context without changing model weights and that continual learning remains an open question. It does not state that converting harness-supplied memory into an intrinsic neural-network memory capability has not yet been figured out.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that those harnesses work, and that's exactly what makes them a little dangerous as a way of thinking about the problem. If you give a model a scratchpad, a retrieval system, a tool that checks its work, you get real gains. But what you've done is built a scaffold around a weakness rather than removing the weakness, and scaffolds have a way of becoming load-bearing.

Coming from protein structure, the analogy I keep reaching for is the old pipeline approach. Before AlphaFold, you'd have a system of hand-built stages: a homology search here, a fragment library there, a physics-based refinement at the end. Each piece compensated for something the others couldn't do, and each piece was individually sensible. But the errors didn't cancel, they compounded, and more importantly the pipeline couldn't learn from its own failures end to end. The information about why a prediction was wrong never flowed back to the parts that caused it. What actually worked was letting one system see the whole problem and carry the uncertainty through, rather than collapsing it at every interface.

I worry that external memory for agents has the same flavor. When you write something to a memory store and read it back later, you've serialized a rich internal state into text and thrown away most of what the model actually knew about that moment, including how confident it was and what alternatives it was holding. The retrieval step is then a lossy, heuristic process the model doesn't really control. So you get an agent that can technically recall a fact from three hours ago but has lost the context that made that fact meaningful. That's not quite memory in the sense a person has it.

The other limitation is that the harness encodes the designer's theory of what the model is bad at, and that theory goes stale fast. Every six months the model gets better at something you built a crutch for, and now the crutch is in the way. It constrains the behavior to the shape you anticipated, and the interesting capabilities are usually the ones nobody anticipated.

So I don't think harnesses are wrong. They're how you ship something useful today, and I'd use them. But I'd treat them as measurements of where the model is still deficient, a kind of running list of what we haven't yet figured out how to put inside the model, rather than as the architecture. The bet I'd make is that the durable progress comes from whatever makes the harness unnecessary.

r001.rationale: The response describes external memory as a harness capability and says harnesses track what has not yet been figured out how to put inside the model. This communicates the gap between harness-supplied memory and an intrinsic model capability.

astra-6.text:
I think the limitation is that you can give a model somewhere to write things down, but that doesn’t necessarily give it the ability to use what it’s written down. It still has to decide what matters, when to retrieve it, and whether that information should change its plan.

And you can put more of those decisions into the software around it. That can be very useful. But then the question is how much of the competence is in the model and how much is in your assumptions about the task. If the harness anticipates the failure, it can catch it. What happens when you encounter a failure you didn’t anticipate?

So I wouldn’t dismiss these approaches. Memory and tools are clearly valuable. I just think there’s a distinction between giving a system the resources to solve a problem and giving it the judgment to use those resources. The scaffolding doesn’t automatically solve the second part.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes external memory and harness resources from the model’s ability to use them, but does not state that we have not figured out how to distill harness-supplied memory into an intrinsic neural-network memory capability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the limitation is that you can give a system somewhere to write things down, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it knows what to write down, when to retrieve it, or how to use it. Those are part of the intelligence you’re trying to build in the first place.

An external memory can preserve the result of a calculation, but it can also preserve a mistake. And if the model can’t reliably distinguish the two, you haven’t solved the underlying problem; you’ve given it a way to carry that problem forward.

That doesn’t mean these systems aren’t useful. They clearly are. But I’d be cautious about assuming that enough machinery around a model will compensate for any weakness in the model itself. At some point, the system still has to make a good decision about what to do next.

r001.rationale: The response says external memory does not fix the model’s weaknesses in deciding what to store, retrieve, or use. It does not state that we have not figured out how to distill harness-supplied memory into the neural network’s intrinsic memory capability.
